demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I acted in ways that go against who I am
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: The trauma type is accidentally causing serious injury to another person. 'Memory Feels Alien' can occur in PTSD, but paired with the available appraisal pattern it suggests stronger dissociation/self-detachment than is otherwise represented; more importantly, the memory cluster centers on fragmented visual recall and rage, whereas the appraisal cluster centers on guilt/meaning plus personal bodily damage, making the profile feel pulled between different trauma experiences.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma type, which is causing serious injury to another person rather than being physically injured oneself. Unless the event also seriously injured the patient, this item is clinically implausible. It also does not fit well with the Memory → Negative Appraisals formulation, because the memory items provided more naturally support guilt, shame, or moral injury appraisals such as 'Violated Values' rather than permanent bodily damage.

vignette:
Raj had always taken a quiet pride in his work. For fifteen years, he had cleaned the homes of others with a meticulousness that was its own form of meditation. At 52, divorced and living alone, the order he brought to these spaces was the primary source of order in his own life. That was before the accident six months ago, an event that did not unfold in his mind as a story but as a slideshow of frozen, searing moments.

It happened in the foyer of the Miller house, a cavernous space of white marble he had just finished mopping. He had placed the yellow "Wet Floor" sign at the entrance to the hall, a familiar ritual. He was coiling the cord of the buffer when he heard the light, quick patter of small feet. The Millers' five-year-old daughter, laughing as she chased a small red ball, paid no mind to the sign. The memory of what happened next is not a sequence for Raj, but three distinct, silent photographs that ambush him without warning. The first is the red ball rolling past his feet. The second is the child's leg angled unnaturally as she slipped. The third, the one that wakes him at night, is her small body crumpled at the base of a heavy console table, a dark stain blossoming on the floor beside her head.

Now, Raj's work is a minefield of reminders. The scent of pine disinfectant, the sight of a yellow plastic sign, or the simple act of wringing out a mop can instantly bring one of the images to the forefront of his mind. These are not memories he can control; they are assaults. And when they come, they bring with them a hot, familiar fury that rises in his chest, a rage directed entirely at himself. The snapshot of the child's sneaker, lying on its side next to her still form, will flash into his mind while he is scrubbing a countertop. With it comes the immediate, sickening certainty: This happened because of you. Because of how you acted. This thought is not a fleeting self-criticism but a profound verdict on his character. He had always seen himself as a careful, gentle man; the memory serves as undeniable proof that he had violated his most fundamental values, that he was, in fact, a person who brings harm to the innocent.

This cycle of intrusive images and crushing self-blame has hollowed out his life. Each remembered snapshot reinforces his belief that he is unforgivable, and this belief drains all purpose from his days. Nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore, not the praise of a client, not a phone call with his sister, not the taste of his own cooking. It all feels like a charade, the hollow performance of a man who should have no right to simple pleasures. The connection between the memory and his appraisal of himself is absolute; the images are the evidence, and the verdict is a life sentence of worthlessness. He has started refusing jobs in homes with children, a decision that has significantly cut his income and earned him a warning from his agency. His ex-wife, with whom he had shared a quiet friendship since their divorce, now finds him sullen and unreachable, the self-loathing a wall between them.

Raj has come to therapy not because he believes he deserves to feel better, but because he is terrified of losing his job, the last remaining structure in his life. He explained that the torment of the memories is constant, but what scares him more is the thought of them fading. Forgetting, he feels, would be the final, unforgivable act. He is trapped between the agony of remembering and the perceived moral failure of moving on, convinced that his suffering is the only thing of meaning he has left.
